related_questions.question: What should you eat when you have inflammatory bowel disease?

text_blocks.snippet: A balanced and nutritious diet is crucial for managing Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), with the Mediterranean diet being a good starting point due to its anti-inflammatory properties and emphasis on whole foods. Specific carbohydrate and exclusion diets are also popular, but individual triggers and tolerances vary. Working with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian is recommended to personalize dietary strategies.
snippet_highlighted_words: Mediterranean diet being a good starting point due to its anti-inflammatory properties and emphasis on whole foods

list.title: Focus on whole, unprocessed foods:
list.snippet: Fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and healthy fats are generally well-tolerated and beneficial.

list.title: Limit processed foods, red meat, and added sugars:
list.snippet: These can exacerbate inflammation in some individuals.

list.title: Consider a Mediterranean-style diet:
list.snippet: This diet is rich in fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and healthy fats, and is often recommended for its anti-inflammatory benefits.

list.title: Pay attention to food tolerances and triggers:
list.snippet: Spicy foods, alcohol, caffeine, and certain high-fiber foods can worsen symptoms for some.

list.title: Small, frequent meals may be easier to digest:
list.snippet: This can help manage symptoms during active flares.

list.title: Consider a low-FODMAP diet:
list.snippet: This diet may help reduce symptoms of functional gut issues, according to the Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine.

list.title: Consider a gluten-free diet:
list.snippet: Some individuals with IBD find that eliminating gluten improves their symptoms, according to Everyday Health.

list.title: Probiotics and Prebiotics:
list.snippet: Foods like yogurt, kefir, and fermented vegetables (probiotics) and foods high in soluble fiber (prebiotics) can help support gut health.
Specific Carbohydrate Diet (SCD): This diet focuses on simple carbohydrates and unprocessed foods.
IBD-Anti-Inflammatory Diet (IBD-AID): This diet combines elements of the SCD with a focus on restoring gut flora balance through prebiotics and probiotics.
Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet (CDED): This diet aims to limit or exclude foods that may negatively affect the gut microbiome, inflammation, and nutrient absorption.

list.title: Individualized approach:
list.snippet: What works for one person with IBD may not work for another.

list.title: Working with a healthcare professional:
list.snippet: Consulting with a doctor or registered dietitian is essential to develop a safe and effective dietary plan.

list.title: Gradual introduction of foods:
list.snippet: When adding new foods back into the diet after a flare, do so slowly and monitor for any symptom changes.

list.title: Nutrient deficiencies:
list.snippet: IBD can sometimes lead to nutrient deficiencies, so supplementation may be necessary, according to CommonSpirit Health.

related_questions.question: What is the difference between IBS and inflammatory bowel disease?

text_blocks.snippet: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) are both gastrointestinal conditions, but they differ significantly in their nature and impact. IBD, which includes conditions like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, involves chronic inflammation and potential damage to the digestive tract. In contrast, IBS is a functional disorder, meaning it doesn't cause visible inflammation or damage but affects how the digestive system works.
snippet_highlighted_words: IBD, which includes conditions like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, involves chronic inflammation and potential damage to the digestive tract.
In contrast, IBS is a functional disorder, meaning it doesn't cause visible inflammation or damage but affects how the digestive system works

list.title: Inflammation:
list.snippet: IBD is characterized by chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, which can lead to ulcers, sores, and tissue damage.

list.title: Types:
list.snippet: Common types of IBD include Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Symptoms can include abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloody stools, weight loss, fatigue, and fever.

list.title: Damage:
list.snippet: IBD can cause structural damage to the digestive tract, requiring medical intervention.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: IBD treatment focuses on reducing inflammation and managing symptoms, often with medications like anti-inflammatories, immune system suppressors, and biologics.

list.title: Functional Disorder:
list.snippet: IBS is a functional disorder, meaning it affects how the digestive system functions without causing inflammation or damage.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: IBS symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, gas, diarrhea, and constipation.

list.title: No Damage:
list.snippet: Unlike IBD, IBS does not cause visible damage to the digestive tract.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: IBS treatment focuses on managing symptoms and identifying triggers like diet, stress, and certain medications.

related_questions.question: What does IBD pain feel like?

text_blocks.snippet: IBD pain can manifest as sharp abdominal cramping, and/or pain in the rectum. It can also include pain from constipation and may be accompanied by fatigue, weight loss, and urgent bowel movements. The pain can be felt in different areas of the abdomen, depending on the specific type and location of inflammation within the digestive tract.
snippet_highlighted_words: sharp abdominal cramping, and/or pain in the rectum

list.snippet: Location: IBD pain can be felt in various areas of the abdomen, including the lower right quadrant, middle lower abdomen, or even the upper abdomen, depending on the affected areas of the digestive tract according to Verywell Health and Bay Area Gastroenterology Associates, LLC.
Type: The pain can range from a sharp cramp to a dull ache.
Other symptoms: IBD pain can be accompanied by other symptoms like fatigue, weight loss, and urgent bowel movements, which may be explosive.
Impact: The pain can be debilitating, affecting daily activities, and leading to anxiety, frustration, and even depression, says the Mayo Clinic.
Variations: Pain can be constant or intermittent, and may worsen during flare-ups.
Non-gastrointestinal symptoms: IBD can also cause pain and inflammation in other areas, such as joints, skin, and eyes.

text_blocks.snippet: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in horses is a group of intestinal disorders characterized by the abnormal infiltration of inflammatory cells into the intestinal wall, leading to malabsorption and maldigestion. This can result in weight loss, colic, and diarrhea, though the severity and specific symptoms can vary. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy, biopsy, and blood work, while treatment may include immunosuppressants, dietary changes, and in some cases, surgery.
snippet_highlighted_words: a group of intestinal disorders characterized by the abnormal infiltration of inflammatory cells into the intestinal wall, leading to malabsorption and maldigestion

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Horses with IBD may exhibit weight loss, recurrent colic, lethargy, and dependent edema (fluid accumulation). Diarrhea may or may not be present.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Definitive diagnosis requires intestinal biopsy, often obtained through endoscopy of the small intestine. Blood work and absorption tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test, can also be helpful.

list.title: Types of IBD:
list.snippet: IBD in horses is classified based on the type of inflammatory cells that infiltrate the intestine: granulomatous, lymphocytic-plasmacytic, or eosinophilic, according to Veterinary Clinics: Equine Practice.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment options include corticosteroids (like prednisolone or dexamethasone) to reduce inflammation, dietary modifications (such as switching to a pelleted diet or hay pellets), and in rare cases, surgical removal of affected bowel sections.

list.title: Prognosis:
list.snippet: The prognosis for horses with IBD varies depending on the extent and severity of the disease, as well as the initial response to treatment.

list.title: Possible Causes:
list.snippet: While the exact cause of IBD in horses is not fully understood, it is thought to involve an abnormal immune response to antigens, potentially from food, parasites, or bacteria.

list.title: Risk Factors:
list.snippet: Stress, recent hospitalization, transportation, previous intestinal impactions, parasite burden, fasting, and contact with infected horses or environments can be risk factors.

list.title: Distinguishing from other conditions:
list.snippet: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) should be distinguished from Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), which is a different condition with overlapping symptoms says the CDC.
